hints: Look at the displacement at $t=0$ on the given graph - is the particle at equilibrium or at maximum displacement, and what does that mean for its speed?
Recall $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ where $v$ is the gradient of the displacement-time graph, so $KE$ is zero at the displacement peaks and maximum when displacement is zero.
Count how many times displacement is zero in time $2T$ - each zero crossing gives a $KE$ maximum, so compare the number of humps in graphs A and B with graphs C and D.
walkthrough: The displacement-time graph shows simple harmonic vibration with period $T$. At $t=0$ the displacement is at a negative maximum, and at $t=T$ and $t=2T$ it is again at a maximum magnitude.
Velocity is the gradient of displacement against time. At maximum displacement the gradient is zero, so $v=0$. At zero displacement the gradient is steepest, so speed is maximum.
Kinetic energy is $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. Therefore $KE = 0$ when $x$ is maximum, and $KE$ is maximum when $x = 0$. Also $KE$ can never be negative.
At $t=0$ the particle has $v=0$, so the $KE$-time graph must start at zero. This rules out the graphs that start at a maximum.
In one displacement period $T$ the particle passes through $x=0$ twice, once moving each way. So $KE$ reaches maximum twice per $T$, meaning four maxima in time $2T$.
Only the graph starting at zero with four equal humps in $2T$, touching zero at each maximum displacement, satisfies both conditions. This is option D.

A.explanation: Starts with maximum kinetic energy at $t=0$, but the displacement graph shows maximum displacement at $t=0$ where speed and kinetic energy are zero.

B.explanation: Starts at zero which is correct, but shows only one kinetic energy cycle per period $T$, whereas kinetic energy is maximum twice per oscillation.

C.explanation: Has the correct double frequency with four peaks in time $2T$, but starts with maximum kinetic energy at $t=0$ instead of zero.

D.explanation: Starts at zero at $t=0$ and peaks each time displacement is zero, giving two kinetic energy maxima per period $T$ with $KE \ge 0$.
